newsitem.title: KENYA: Go-slow chaos for Kenya flights, shilling weakens.
newsitem.headline: Go-slow chaos for Kenya flights, shilling weakens.

text.p: Pressures on Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi's government grew on Monday as the third day of an air traffic controllers' go-slow brought chaos to flights and the shilling weakened further against the dollar.

The government made a proposal to end the protest by air traffic controllers and its attorney-general unveiled plans to review the constitution. But his protracted timetable fell far short of opposition demands.
A third day of the protest by controllers delayed passenger and cargo flights for up to 12 hours at one of the year's busiest periods for one of Africa's main tourist destinations.

The Kenyan shilling's international value slid on Monday with high dollar demand after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) halted a $205 million aid package on Thursday because of high-level corruption.
"The go-slow is in its third day and it is absolute chaos out there," said an air traffic controller at Kenyatta Airport.
An airport official said air traffic controllers were later given a government proposal under which they would return to work and give authorities two weeks to consider their demands.
National carrier Kenya Airways said planes leaving Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta airport were delayed by between three and 12 hours and arriving flights were waiting up to two hours to land.
Air traffic controllers who say they earn about $90 a month began a go-slow at midnight on Friday, demanding a 50-fold pay increase, housing allowances and government-backed mortgages.
Jomo Kenyatta is the main cargo and passenger hub for East Africa and for some air cargo carriers is even more important than airports in South Africa, the continent's economic leader.
Meteorologists who supply weather information have launched a go-slow, increasing problems in flying in all of East Africa.
Air cargo giant Lufthansa Cargo said the go-slow could cost the industry millions of dollars if it continued much longer.

Airlink said it stood to lose completely a cargo of five tonnes of fresh flowers, awaiting a connection to South Africa since Saturday. Tourism is Kenya's biggest hard currency earner with flowers and fresh produce in fourth place.
Ironically, Kenyan exporters led by flower growers and tourism companies have pressed since 1994 for a weaker shilling, saying its previous strong value made them uncompetitive.
The shilling weakened to close at 63, 3.25 percent down from Monday's opening, according to commercial bank rates.
There was no activity on the foreign board at the Nairobi Stock Exchange and nervous foreign investors offloaded Central Bank of Kenya floating-rate treasury bonds.
Moi, 73 and Kenya's ruler for 19 years, hit out on Sunday at the IMF decision to cancel the loan, saying the reasons were political and ordinary Kenyans would be hurt.
An alliance of opposition-backed groups pressing the government for political reforms before a general election later this year has called for a national general strike on Friday.
Attorney-General Amos Wako published a draft bill on Monday to create a commission to review the constitution and said it had up to three years to report to Moi, 73 and in power for 19 years.
"This is too long, too long," said Peter Anyang' Nyong'o, a member of parliament for the opposition FORD-Kenya party and a member of the National Convention Executive Committee pushing for reforms.
"The commission could do its work in a year. A lot of work has already been done. The government is time-wasting," he said.

Joseph Koech, a minister of state in the president's office who said on Friday he had quit, said on Monday he had changed his mind because of supporters' pressure and urged the sacking of civil servants whose lax attitude prompted the IMF move.
